"Develop a complete RUGBY WORLD CUP GAME designed exclusively for mobile devices (Android and iOS).

CORE VISION:
Create a realistic, highly playable rugby union simulation with the Rugby World Cup as its central competition. Prioritise gameplay systems, realistic physics, player behaviour, match mechanics and tactical depth over high-end graphics.

The game should feel like an authentic international rugby experience, with accessible mobile controls and surprisingly deep gameplay.

1. WORLD CUP TOURNAMENT SYSTEM

- Full Rugby World Cup tournament structure.
- International teams from around the world.
- Official-style group stages, standings, points tables and knockout rounds.
- Quarter-finals, semi-finals, third-place playoff and grand final.
- Tournament draws and dynamically generated fixtures.
- Team qualification and tournament progression.
- Trophy presentation and championship celebrations.
- Historical tournament mode where players can recreate previous World Cups.
- Custom tournament mode allowing players to create their own competitions.

2. REALISTIC RUGBY PHYSICS – TOP PRIORITY

Build a physics-driven rugby gameplay system.

- Realistic player momentum, acceleration, deceleration and turning.
- Different player weights, heights, strength and speed affecting movement.
- Realistic collisions between players.
- Dynamic tackling based on positioning, momentum, timing and player strength.
- Different tackle animations and outcomes.
- Players should stumble, fall, get pushed backwards or break through tackles depending on physics and attributes.
- Realistic ball movement, passing trajectories, bouncing and kicking.
- Ball physics must react naturally to the ground, players and collisions.
- Realistic player balance and recovery after contact.
- Rucks should form naturally after tackles.
- Dynamic player positioning around breakdowns.
- Realistic offloads and one-handed passes where appropriate.

Avoid scripted interactions wherever possible. Gameplay should be driven by player attributes, positioning, timing and physics.

3. COMPLETE RUGBY UNION MECHANICS

Implement proper 15-a-side rugby union rules and gameplay:

- Scrums with pushing contests and team strength calculations.
- Lineouts with jumping, lifting and throwing mechanics.
- Rucks and mauls.
- Tackles and tackle turnovers.
- Passing backwards and lateral passing.
- Offloads.
- Breakaway runs.
- Kicking for territory.
- Grubber kicks.
- Cross-field kicks.
- Box kicks.
- Tactical kicking.
- Conversions.
- Penalty kicks.
- Drop goals.
- Try scoring.
- Advantage rules.
- Knock-ons.
- Forward passes.
- Offside rules.
- Sin bins and red cards.
- Substitutions.
- Referee decisions and match penalties.

The rules should be consistent and enforced by the game engine.

4. PLAYER ATTRIBUTES AND POSITIONS

Every player must have individual attributes that affect gameplay.

Attributes include:

- Speed
- Acceleration
- Strength
- Stamina
- Agility
- Tackling
- Passing
- Kicking
- Ball handling
- Jumping
- Scrummaging
- Positioning
- Awareness
- Discipline

Create all 15 rugby positions, each with unique responsibilities and gameplay characteristics.

Player attributes should influence animations, physics, AI behaviour and match performance.

5. INTELLIGENT OPPONENT AI

Create advanced rugby AI that understands rugby tactics.

- AI players should maintain realistic formations.
- Forwards should support rucks, scrums and mauls.
- Backs should create attacking opportunities.
- Players should intelligently run support lines.
- AI should recognise gaps in defensive lines.
- Defenders should coordinate tackles and cover.
- AI should decide when to pass, kick, run or offload.
- Teams should adapt their tactics depending on the score and remaining match time.
- Strong teams should demonstrate better decision-making, not simply boosted statistics.

Each national team should have its own playing style.

6. MOBILE GAMEPLAY AND CONTROLS

Designed specifically for touchscreen devices.

Create intuitive controls:

- Virtual movement joystick.
- Pass buttons with directional passing.
- Sprint button.
- Tackle button.
- Offload button.
- Kick button with kick selection.
- Special tactical actions.
- Context-sensitive scrum and lineout controls.

Controls should be responsive, easy to understand and configurable.

Include different control layouts and adjustable sensitivity.

Avoid overcrowding the screen. Controls should adapt to the player's current situation, whether attacking, defending, kicking or participating in set pieces.

7. GRAPHICS AND PRESENTATION

Do NOT prioritise ultra-realistic graphics.

Instead:

- Use optimised, clean poly 3D mobile graphics.
- Create recognisable player models and rugby animations.
- Make stadiums feel alive without excessive environmental detail.
- Include crowds, goalposts, advertising boards, referees and team benches.
- Create realistic rugby kits and national colours.
- Use dynamic camera angles during tries, kicks and important moments.
- Include simple but polished stadium lighting.
- Ensure smooth performance on mid-range Android devices.

The game must be designed for mobile hardware, not adapted from a demanding PC or console game.

8. CAREER AND TEAM MANAGEMENT

Include a career mode where players can manage an international rugby team.

- Select starting XV and substitutes.
- Manage player fitness and stamina.
- Develop young players.
- Improve individual attributes.
- Manage injuries and suspensions.
- Choose attacking and defensive strategies.
- Select team formations and tactical approaches.
- Build team chemistry.
- Unlock historical players and legendary teams where appropriate.

9. MATCH PRESENTATION

Make matches feel like proper international rugby broadcasts.

- National anthems before major matches.
- Team entrances.
- Stadium atmosphere.
- Match clock and scoreboard.
- Half-time presentation.
- Try celebrations.
- Referee whistle and match commentary.
- Full-time celebrations.
- World Cup trophy presentation.

10. GAME MODES

Include:

- World Cup Tournament.
- Quick Match.
- Career Mode.
- Historical World Cups.
- Custom Tournament.
- Training Mode.
- Practice Matches.
- Exhibition Mode.

11. TECHNICAL AND PERFORMANCE REQUIREMENTS

- Mobile-only development.
- Optimise for Android and iOS.
- Prioritise stable frame rates and responsive controls.
- Use efficient 3D models and animations.
- Optimise physics calculations for mobile hardware.
- Use modular gameplay systems.
- Ensure AI and physics work together correctly.
- Save tournament and career progress.
- Create fully functional menus and navigation.

MOST IMPORTANT DEVELOPMENT INSTRUCTION

Do not sacrifice gameplay systems for visual quality.

The three biggest priorities are:

1. Physics: Realistic collisions, tackling, momentum, ball movement and player interactions.
2. Gameplay: Fully functional rugby mechanics, proper rules, set pieces and tactical options.
3. AI: Intelligent teammates and opponents who understand rugby and behave like real rugby players.

Build a playable, fully functional rugby game rather than a visual prototype. Every major button, game mode and gameplay mechanic must actually work.

The final experience should feel like a compact but deep rugby simulation made specifically for mobile devices.

---
This is a build request. Build a complete, playable game now (or apply the requested change to the existing game). Do not ask clarifying questions; make reasonable assumptions and note them briefly when you finish.

Screenshots for your own checks: save small JPEGs (a .jpg path, viewport at most 1280px wide) and read only the latest one; older images are dropped from context. Read a full-size PNG only when fine detail matters.
"

function rngFrom(seed) {
  let a = seed >>> 0;
  return () => {
    a |= 0; a = a + 0x6D2B79F5 | 0;
    let t = Math.imul(a ^ a >>> 15, 1 | a);
    t = t + Math.imul(t ^ t >>> 7, 61 | t) ^ t;
    return ((t ^ t >>> 14) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
  };
}
export { rngFrom };

export function hashString(s) {
  let h = 2166136261;
  for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) { h ^= s.charCodeAt(i); h = Math.imul(h, 16777619); }
  return h >>> 0;
}

export function overallFor(player) {
  const p = player.position || 'IC';
  const weights = {
    LHP:{strength:.24,scrum:.26,tackling:.14,stamina:.12,discipline:.1,agility:.06,speed:.04,awareness:.04},
    HK:{strength:.18,scrum:.2,tackling:.16,stamina:.12,awareness:.1,agility:.08,handling:.08,discipline:.08},

    FB:{speed:.16,kicking:.15,handling:.14,positioning:.15,awareness:.14,tackling:.1,agility:.08,passing:.05,discipline:.03},

    CTR:{speed:.16,agility:.15,passing:.12,tackling:.12,strength:.1,handling:.1,awareness:.1,positioning:.08,discipline:.07}
  }[p] || { speed:.1, strength:.1, passing:.1, tackling:.1, awareness:.1, handling:.1, agility:.1, kicking:.1, stamina:.1, discipline:.1, positioning:.1 };
  let total = 0, w = 0;

}

const clamp = (v,a=35,b=99) => Math.max(a, Math.min(b, Math.round(v)));

export function makeSquad(team, seedExtra = 0, options = {}) {
  const rng = rngFrom(hashString(team.id + ':' + seedExtra));
  const firsts = FIRSTS[team.pool] || FIRSTS.en;
  const lasts = SURNAMES[team.pool] || SURNAMES.en;
  const used = new Set();
  return POSITIONS.map((pos, idx) => {
    let first, last, name;
    do {
      first = firsts[Math.floor(rng() * firsts.length)];
      last = lasts[Math.floor(rng() * lasts.length)];
      name = `${first} ${last}`;
    } while (used.has(name));
    used.add(name);
    const prof = POSITION_PROFILE[pos.key] || POSITION_PROFILE.CTR;
    const base = team.rating - 4 + rng() * 8;
    const attrs = {};
    for (const a of ATTRS) {
      let v = base + (prof[a] || 0) + (rng() - .5) * 10;
      if (pos.group === 'BEN') v -= 3;
      attrs[a] = clamp(v);
    }
    attrs.stamina = clamp(attrs.stamina + 4, 40, 99);
    const player = {
      id: `${team.id}-${idx + 1}`,
      teamId: team.id,
      number: pos.n,
      position: pos.key,
      posName: pos.name,
      group: pos.group === 'BEN' ? 'BEN' : pos.group,
      name,
      age: 21 + Math.floor(rng() * 13),
      height: 176 + Math.floor(rng() * 30),
      weight: pos.group === 'FWD' ? 102 + Math.floor(rng() * 23) : 80 + Math.floor(rng() * 20),
      potential: clamp(72 + rng() * 22, 70, 99),
      ...attrs,
      form: 70 + Math.floor(rng() * 22),
      fitness: 88 + Math.floor(rng() * 12),
      morale: 75 + Math.floor(rng() * 20),
      xp: 0,
      injury: 0,
      suspension: 0,
      starter: pos.n <= 15,
      bench: pos.n > 15
    };
    player.overall = overallFor(player);
    return player;
  });
}

export function teamRating(team, squad) {
  if (!squad?.length) return team.rating;
  const starters = squad.filter(p => p.number <= 15);
  return Math.round(starters.reduce((s,p) => s + (p.overall || overallFor(p)), 0) / Math.max(1,starters.length));
}

export function teamLineup(squad) {
  const starters = squad.filter(p => p.number <= 15 && !p.injury && !p.suspension);
  if (starters.length === 15) return starters.sort((a,b)=>a.number-b.number);
  return squad.filter(p => p.number <= 15).sort((a,b)=>a.number-b.number);
}

## Objective
- Build a complete, playable, mobile-first Rugby World Cup game with authentic 15-a-side rugby, tournament and career systems, physics-driven play, AI tactics, and accessible touch controls.

## Requirements
- Mobile-only Android/iOS experience with clean, performant 3D-inspired presentation.
- Gameplay and rules must take priority over graphics.
- Include World Cup, historical/custom tournaments, quick match, career, practice, training, and exhibition modes.
- Implement physics, set pieces, rucks/mauls, tackling, kicking, scoring, penalties, cards, substitutions, AI formations, and management systems.
- Save progress and provide responsive, configurable mobile controls.

## Decisions
- Use an original mobile-first web implementation with HTML, CSS, Canvas, and JavaScript modules.
- Use deterministic, ratings-and-physics-flavoured rugby simulation rather than a demanding full 3D engine.
- Generate no-asset audio and original Web Audio fanfares to keep the experience lightweight.
- Implement tournament and career save state in browser storage.

## Work State
### Completed
- Created the main application shell and responsive interface.
- Implemented team, player, position, attribute, squad, stadium, historic edition, and legend data.
- Implemented the rugby match engine, including momentum, player movement, passing, kicking, tackles, rucks, set-piece hooks, scoring, cards, advantage, penalties, training drills, and match clock.
- Implemented Canvas match rendering with top-down presentation, stadium atmosphere, players, ball, cameras, try moments, and broadcast-style overlays.
- Implemented tournament draw, group/knockout progression, standings, fixture advancement, simulation, historical tournaments, custom tournaments, and trophy presentation.
- Implemented career generation, schedule, table, squad management, player development, lineup selection, training, and season progression.
- Implemented Web Audio feedback for whistles, kicks, tackles, tries, crowds, and fanfares.
- Added mobile match controls, menus, settings, training UI, career UI, tournament UI, and match presentation styling.
- Attempted syntax checks for the engine, tournament, data, and renderer modules.

### Active
- Final integration verification and browser testing remain unfinished.
- Match UI/action wiring and end-to-end mode verification need broader testing.
- Some engine and renderer integration issues may remain despite syntax-level checks.

### Blocked
- Browser visual and interaction testing could not be confirmed by an available screenshot in the provided conversation.
- No explicit remaining runtime bug list was established.

## Next Move
1. Start the local app and verify it loads in a mobile viewport.
2. Exercise navigation across Home, Match, Tournament, Career, Training, and Settings.
3. Start Quick Match and verify controls, passing, kicking, tackling, scoring, pause, and full-time flows.
4. Run a tournament through group stages and knockout rounds.
5. Run career fixture, lineup, development, training, and season flows.
6. Capture and inspect a final mobile screenshot; fix any layout, runtime, or console issues.

## Relevant Files
- `/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/index.html`: Application entry point.
- `/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/styles.css`: Complete responsive styling and mobile layouts.
- `/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/js/app.js`: Main menu, navigation, tournament, career, training, settings, and match UI orchestration.
- `/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/js/engine.js`: Core rugby simulation, physics-flavoured match mechanics, AI, rules, set pieces, scoring, and match state.
- `/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/js/renderer.js`: Canvas match rendering and broadcast presentation.
- `/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/js/data.js`: Teams, players, positions, attributes, stadiums, historic editions, and legends.
- `/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/js/tournament.js`: Tournament structure, draws, fixtures, standings, progression, and simulation.
- `/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/js/career.js`: Career squads, fixtures, table, training, player development, and season creation.
- `/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/js/audio.js`: Web Audio effects and fanfares.

## Important Context
- `js/engine.js` exports `simulateMatch()` for non-live fixture simulation.
- The implementation is a browser/mobile web app rather than a native Android or iOS binary.
- Match presentation and controls are centralized through `MatchRenderer` and `RugbyGame`.
- The next agent should begin with runtime verification and console inspection, as the implementation is extensive and integration testing is incomplete.

"Develop a complete RUGBY WORLD CUP GAME designed exclusively for mobile devices (Android and iOS).

CORE VISION:
Create a realistic, highly playable rugby union simulation with the Rugby World Cup as its central competition. Prioritise gameplay systems, realistic physics, player behaviour, match mechanics and tactical depth over high-end graphics.

The game should feel like an authentic international rugby experience, with accessible mobile controls and surprisingly deep gameplay.

1. WORLD CUP TOURNAMENT SYSTEM

- Full Rugby World Cup tournament structure.
- International teams from around the world.
- Official-style group stages, standings, points tables and knockout rounds.
- Quarter-finals, semi-finals, third-place playoff and grand final.
- Tournament draws and dynamically generated fixtures.
- Team qualification and tournament progression.
- Trophy presentation and championship celebrations.
- Historical tournament mode where players can recreate previous World Cups.
- Custom tournament mode allowing players to create their own competitions.

2. REALISTIC RUGBY PHYSICS – TOP PRIORITY

Build a physics-driven rugby gameplay system.

- Realistic player momentum, acceleration, deceleration and turning.
- Different player weights, heights, strength and speed affecting movement.
- Realistic collisions between players.
- Dynamic tackling based on positioning, momentum, timing and player strength.
- Different tackle animations and outcomes.
- Players should stumble, fall, get pushed backwards or break through tackles depending on physics and attributes.
- Realistic ball movement, passing trajectories, bouncing and kicking.
- Ball physics must react naturally to the ground, players and collisions.
- Realistic player balance and recovery after contact.
- Rucks should form naturally after tackles.
- Dynamic player positioning around breakdowns.
- Realistic offloads and one-handed passes where appropriate.

Avoid scripted interactions wherever possible. Gameplay should be driven by player attributes, positioning, timing and physics.

3. COMPLETE RUGBY UNION MECHANICS

Implement proper 15-a-side rugby union rules and gameplay:

- Scrums with pushing contests and team strength calculations.
- Lineouts with jumping, lifting and throwing mechanics.
- Rucks and mauls.
- Tackles and tackle turnovers.
- Passing backwards and lateral passing.
- Offloads.
- Breakaway runs.
- Kicking for territory.
- Grubber kicks.
- Cross-field kicks.
- Box kicks.
- Tactical kicking.
- Conversions.
- Penalty kicks.
- Drop goals.
- Try scoring.
- Advantage rules.
- Knock-ons.
- Forward passes.
- Offside rules.
- Sin bins and red cards.
- Substitutions.
- Referee decisions and match penalties.

The rules should be consistent and enforced by the game engine.

4. PLAYER ATTRIBUTES AND POSITIONS

Every player must have individual attributes that affect gameplay.

Attributes include:

- Speed
- Acceleration
- Strength
- Stamina
- Agility
- Tackling
- Passing
- Kicking
- Ball handling
- Jumping
- Scrummaging
- Positioning
- Awareness
- Discipline

Create all 15 rugby positions, each with unique responsibilities and gameplay characteristics.

Player attributes should influence animations, physics, AI behaviour and match performance.

5. INTELLIGENT OPPONENT AI

Create advanced rugby AI that understands rugby tactics.

- AI players should maintain realistic formations.
- Forwards should support rucks, scrums and mauls.
- Backs should create attacking opportunities.
- Players should intelligently run support lines.
- AI should recognise gaps in defensive lines.
- Defenders should coordinate tackles and cover.
- AI should decide when to pass, kick, run or offload.
- Teams should adapt their tactics depending on the score and remaining match time.
- Strong teams should demonstrate better decision-making, not simply boosted statistics.

Each national team should have its own playing style.

6. MOBILE GAMEPLAY AND CONTROLS

Designed specifically for touchscreen devices.

Create intuitive controls:

- Virtual movement joystick.
- Pass buttons with directional passing.
- Sprint button.
- Tackle button.
- Offload button.
- Kick button with kick selection.
- Special tactical actions.
- Context-sensitive scrum and lineout controls.

Controls should be responsive, easy to understand and configurable.

Include different control layouts and adjustable sensitivity.

Avoid overcrowding the screen. Controls should adapt to the player's current situation, whether attacking, defending, kicking or participating in set pieces.

7. GRAPHICS AND PRESENTATION

Do NOT prioritise ultra-realistic graphics.

Instead:

- Use optimised, clean poly 3D mobile graphics.
- Create recognisable player models and rugby animations.
- Make stadiums feel alive without excessive environmental detail.
- Include crowds, goalposts, advertising boards, referees and team benches.
- Create realistic rugby kits and national colours.
- Use dynamic camera angles during tries, kicks and important moments.
- Include simple but polished stadium lighting.
- Ensure smooth performance on mid-range Android devices.

The game must be designed for mobile hardware, not adapted from a demanding PC or console game.

8. CAREER AND TEAM MANAGEMENT

Include a career mode where players can manage an international rugby team.

- Select starting XV and substitutes.
- Manage player fitness and stamina.
- Develop young players.
- Improve individual attributes.
- Manage injuries and suspensions.
- Choose attacking and defensive strategies.
- Select team formations and tactical approaches.
- Build team chemistry.
- Unlock historical players and legendary teams where appropriate.

9. MATCH PRESENTATION

Make matches feel like proper international rugby broadcasts.

- National anthems before major matches.
- Team entrances.
- Stadium atmosphere.
- Match clock and scoreboard.
- Half-time presentation.
- Try celebrations.
- Referee whistle and match commentary.
- Full-time celebrations.
- World Cup trophy presentation.

10. GAME MODES

Include:

- World Cup Tournament.
- Quick Match.
- Career Mode.
- Historical World Cups.
- Custom Tournament.
- Training Mode.
- Practice Matches.
- Exhibition Mode.

11. TECHNICAL AND PERFORMANCE REQUIREMENTS

- Mobile-only development.
- Optimise for Android and iOS.
- Prioritise stable frame rates and responsive controls.
- Use efficient 3D models and animations.
- Optimise physics calculations for mobile hardware.
- Use modular gameplay systems.
- Ensure AI and physics work together correctly.
- Save tournament and career progress.
- Create fully functional menus and navigation.

MOST IMPORTANT DEVELOPMENT INSTRUCTION

Do not sacrifice gameplay systems for visual quality.

The three biggest priorities are:

1. Physics: Realistic collisions, tackling, momentum, ball movement and player interactions.
2. Gameplay: Fully functional rugby mechanics, proper rules, set pieces and tactical options.
3. AI: Intelligent teammates and opponents who understand rugby and behave like real rugby players.

Build a playable, fully functional rugby game rather than a visual prototype. Every major button, game mode and gameplay mechanic must actually work.

The final experience should feel like a compact but deep rugby simulation made specifically for mobile devices.

This is a build request. Build a complete, playable game now (or apply the requested change to the existing game). Do not ask clarifying questions; make reasonable assumptions and note them briefly when you finish.

Screenshots for your own checks: save small JPEGs (a .jpg path, viewport at most 1280px wide) and read only the latest one; older images are dropped from context. Read a full-size PNG only when fine detail matters.

## Objective
- Continue building and verifying the existing mobile-first Rugby World Cup game, prioritising playable rugby systems, rules, AI, and mobile controls.

## Requirements
- Deliver a playable mobile-focused rugby union game with World Cup, historical/custom tournaments, quick match, career, training, practice, and exhibition modes.
- Prioritise physics-driven gameplay, rugby rules, player attributes, tactical AI, responsive touch controls, and saved progress over high-end graphics.
- Do not ask clarifying questions; make reasonable assumptions.

## Decisions
- Use the existing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript web implementation.
- Keep the lightweight deterministic simulation and Canvas presentation approach.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented the application shell, match engine, Canvas renderer, tournament and career systems, data, audio, and responsive UI, as recorded in the prior checkpoint.
- Ran `node --check` successfully on all `js/*.js` modules.
- Started the app locally and confirmed the home, quick-match setup, pre-match, and live-match screens load in Chromium at a mobile viewport.

### Active
- Continue integration and gameplay verification across navigation, controls, match flows, tournaments, and career.
- Review/fix any runtime or visual issues found during testing.

### Blocked
- No current blocker; Chromium was installed after the initial launch reported it missing.

## Next Move
1. Continue browser testing at mobile dimensions, including touch controls, passing, kicking, tackling, scoring, pause, and full-time flows.
2. Exercise tournament progression and career fixture, lineup, training, and season flows.
3. Investigate any console errors beyond the observed missing `favicon.ico` (404), and fix issues found.
4. Save and inspect a final mobile screenshot.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: App entry point.
- `styles.css`: Responsive styling and mobile layouts.
- `js/app.js`: Navigation, mode UI, match orchestration, and control wiring.
- `js/engine.js`: Match simulation, rules, physics-flavoured mechanics, and AI.
- `js/renderer.js`: Canvas match presentation.
- `js/tournament.js`: Tournament generation and progression.
- `js/career.js`: Career and player development systems.
- `js/data.js`: Teams, players, attributes, and historic editions.
- `js/audio.js`: Web Audio effects and fanfares.

## Important Context
- Local server was started with `python3 -m http.server 3002`; `http://localhost:3002/` returned HTTP 200.
- Browser checks showed the home page and match screens loaded; the only console error observed was `Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 404 (File not found) @ http://localhost:3002/favicon.ico:0`.
- Screenshots were saved as `screenshots/home.png`, `screenshots/quick.png`, `screenshots/prematch.png`, and `screenshots/live1.png`; no code changes or commits were made during these checks.

## Objective
- Build and verify a complete, mobile-first Rugby World Cup game with playable rugby simulation, tournament and career systems, touch controls, and saved progress.

## Requirements
- Mobile-only experience for Android and iOS, prioritizing gameplay, realistic physics, rugby rules, tactical AI, and stable performance.
- Include 15-a-side mechanics, set pieces, tackles, passing, kicking, scoring, cards, substitutions, advantage, and referee decisions.
- Include World Cup, historical/custom tournaments, quick match, career, training, practice, and exhibition modes.
- Use lightweight deterministic Canvas gameplay and efficient mobile presentation rather than high-end graphics.
- Save tournament and career progress locally.

## Decisions
- Continue with the existing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript implementation.
- Retain the deterministic, physics-flavoured Canvas match engine.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented app shell, match engine, renderer, tournament, career, data, audio, navigation, and responsive UI.
- Verified every `js/*.js` module with `node --check`.
- Confirmed the home, quick-match setup, pre-match, and live-match screens at mobile dimensions.
- Completed browser flow testing for kick-off, pause/resume, passing, tackling/action, and kick actions.
- Confirmed the only runtime console resource error observed was a missing `favicon.ico` 404.
- Saved mobile screenshots, including `screenshots/final-mobile.jpg`.

### Active
- Continue integration and gameplay verification across touch controls, scoring, full-time, tournament progression, career progression, and save flows.
- Investigate any runtime or visual issues found beyond the missing favicon.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Exercise tournament and historical/custom tournament progression, draw, standings, fixtures, knockouts, and trophy flows.
2. Exercise career fixture, lineup, substitute, training, tactics, player-development, and season flows.
3. Test full halves, try/conversion/drop-goal/pensalty flows, set pieces, cards, and substitutions.
4. Run console checks and save a latest final mobile screenshot.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: App entry point and mobile metadata.
- `js/app.js`: Navigation, mode orchestration, match controls, and UI actions.
- `js/engine.js`: Match physics, AI, rules, set pieces, and player actions.
- `js/renderer.js`: Canvas match presentation.
- `js/tournament.js`: Tournament generation and knockout progression.
- `js/career.js`: Career, player development, tactics, and season systems.
- `js/data.js`: Teams, players, historical editions, and match data.
- `js/audio.js`: Match audio, crowd, whistles, and fanfares.
- `styles.css`: Mobile-first layouts and match presentation.

## Important Context
- The app is served at `http://localhost:3002/` and that URL returned HTTP 200.
- Browser testing used Chromium at approximately 844×390 viewport dimensions.
- Existing saved screenshots are under `screenshots/`; the latest is `screenshots/final-mobile.jpg`.
- No current code changes or commits were reported during the checkpoint; verify repository status before further edits.

## Objective
- Build and verify a complete, mobile-first Rugby World Cup game with playable rugby simulation, tournament and career systems, touch controls, and saved progress.

## Requirements
- Mobile-first Android/iOS experience prioritizing gameplay, rugby rules, physics, tactical AI, and stable performance.
- Include 15-a-side play, set pieces, tackles, passing, kicking, scoring, cards, substitutions, advantage, and referee decisions.
- Include World Cup, historical/custom tournaments, quick match, career, training, practice, and exhibition modes.
- Use lightweight deterministic Canvas gameplay and save tournament/career progress locally.

## Decisions
- Continue with the existing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript implementation.
- Retain the deterministic, physics-flavoured Canvas match engine.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented the app shell, match engine, renderer, tournament and career systems, data, audio, navigation, and responsive UI.
- Verified all `js/*.js` modules with `node --check`.

- Verify career management tabs and training in the UI, plus full-match scoring, set pieces, cards, and substitutions.

- (none)

1. Reload the app so the updated `js/tournament.js` is active, then run a full tournament UI flow and confirm the final and third-place fixtures both finish.

- `index.html`: App entry point and mobile metadata.

"UPGRADE THE EXISTING RUGBY WORLD CUP GAME WITH THE FOLLOWING SYSTEMS. Do not create a separate game or replace existing working systems. Expand the existing game while preserving all current functionality.

1. HISTORICAL RUGBY DATABASE (1975–PRESENT)

Create a comprehensive historical rugby database covering international rugby from 1975 through to the present day.

Include real historical and modern:

- National teams.
- International players.
- Player names and positions.
- Player statistics and attributes.
- Team statistics and rankings.
- World Cup appearances.
- International caps.
- Tries scored.
- Points scored.
- Kicking statistics.
- Tournament performances.
- Captains and legendary players.

Include legendary players from different generations, alongside current international players.

Examples of players to include:

- Jonah Lomu
- Dan Carter
- Richie McCaw
- Bryan Habana
- Victor Matfield
- Joost van der Westhuizen
- François Pienaar
- Fourie du Preez
- Cheslin Kolbe
- Siya Kolisi
- Antoine Dupont
- Jonny Wilkinson
- Martin Johnson
- Brian O'Driscoll
- Sergio Parisse
- George Gregan
- David Campese
- Gareth Edwards
- JPR Williams

These are examples, not the complete database.

Historical accuracy

- Use real player names and historically accurate statistics wherever verified data is available.
- Player ratings must reflect actual playing abilities during their respective eras.
- Players must have different ratings depending on their career stage.
- A legendary player's prime version should have different attributes from their younger or older versions.
- Historical teams must use appropriate players, kits, team colours and playing styles from their respective periods.
- Include real historical national team squads and tournament rosters wherever data is available.
- Do not invent historical caps, tries, points or achievements.
- Clearly distinguish verified statistics from estimated gameplay ratings.

Allow players to browse historical teams and players by year, country, position and tournament.

2. NATIONAL TEAM IDENTITIES AND PLAYING STYLES

Every national team should have its own identity and tactical approach.

Examples:

SOUTH AFRICA:

- Physical forward play.
- Powerful scrums.
- Strong defensive structures.
- Tactical kicking.
- Dominant breakdown play.

NEW ZEALAND:

- Fast attacking rugby.
- Excellent handling.
- Dynamic running lines.
- Creative offloads.
- High-tempo gameplay.

FRANCE:

- Creative attacking rugby.
- Unpredictable attacking combinations.
- Strong individual flair.

ENGLAND:

- Structured gameplay.
- Strong forward pack.
- Tactical kicking.
- Organised defensive systems.

IRELAND:

- Structured attacking patterns.
- Accurate passing.
- Strong tactical organisation.

These playing styles should influence team AI, tactical tendencies, formations and player behaviour.

3. VERTICAL PORTRAIT GAMEPLAY AND 3D SIDE-VIEW CAMERA

THIS IS A MANDATORY REQUIREMENT.

The game must be played exclusively in VERTICAL PORTRAIT MODE (9:16).

Do not use landscape orientation.

Camera perspective

Create a genuine 3D side-view rugby experience designed around a vertically held mobile phone.

- Use a slightly elevated 3D side-view camera.
- Show players from a side-on perspective rather than looking down from above.
- The pitch should have visible depth and perspective.
- The camera should smoothly follow the active player and ball.
- Allow the camera to scroll along the pitch as the game progresses.
- Keep attacking and defensive players visible wherever possible.
- Use subtle camera zooms during important moments.
- Include cinematic camera adjustments during tries, tackles and major plays.

The game should feel like a 3D rugby simulation viewed from the side, not a 2D rugby game or a top-down strategy game.

Graphics style

Use polished, stylised LOW-POLY 3D graphics.

The graphics should be noticeably better than basic placeholder graphics without requiring photorealistic rendering.

Include:

- Fully modelled 3D rugby players.
- Different body types and physical proportions.
- Recognisable player faces and hairstyles where possible.
- Fully modelled 3D stadiums.
- 3D rugby balls.
- Detailed goalposts.
- Textured rugby pitches.
- Realistic player kits and numbers.
- Stadium crowds.
- Advertising boards.
- Benches and coaching areas.
- Dynamic lighting and shadows.
- Visible grass and pitch markings.

The characters must look like proper 3D human rugby players, not flat sprites or 2D cutouts.

Prioritise smooth performance on mid-range Android devices.

4. COMPLETE MANUAL PLAYER-CONTROL SYSTEM

THIS IS EXTREMELY IMPORTANT.

The user must directly control the players on their team.

Do not make the team play entirely through automatic AI.

Attacking controls

When the user's team has possession:

- The player carrying the ball becomes the actively controlled character.
- The user controls that player's movement using a virtual joystick.
- The user decides when to sprint, change direction, pass, kick or attempt to break through defenders.
- The user controls the direction and timing of passes.
- When the ball is passed, control must automatically transfer to the receiving player once possession is established.
- The receiving player immediately becomes the actively controlled character.
- The user can continue running, passing, kicking or performing other actions with the new ball carrier.

This must happen smoothly and immediately.

Supporting players

Other teammates should still move intelligently, but must not take control away from the user.

- AI teammates should run support lines.
- Players should create attacking space.
- Wingers should stay wide when appropriate.
- Forwards should provide support around breakdowns.
- Teammates should position themselves for offloads and passes.
- AI should recognise opportunities to support the ball carrier.

The user remains in control of the player with the ball.

Defensive controls

When the opposing team has possession:

- Allow the user to switch between all available defensive players.
- Add a dedicated player-switch button.
- Highlight the currently selected defender.
- Allow manual switching using repeated button presses or directional selection.
- The selected player becomes directly controlled by the user.

The user decides how to defend.

Include different defensive actions:

1. NORMAL TACKLE – a standard standing tackle.
2. DIVE TACKLE – a diving attempt to bring down an opponent.
3. LOW TACKLE – targeting the legs.
4. BIG TACKLE – a stronger tackle attempt requiring appropriate timing and positioning.
5. INTERCEPTION – attempting to intercept a pass.
6. DEFENSIVE PRESSURE – closing down the ball carrier.

Different tackling actions must have different animations, physics, success rates and risks.

A poorly timed tackle should have consequences, including missed tackles, broken tackles, players being sidestepped or penalties where appropriate.

Player switching intelligence

- Highlight the currently selected player.
- Make switching responsive.
- Allow quick switching to the nearest relevant defender.
- Never force the user to stay with one defender.
- Switching must not interrupt the flow of gameplay.

5. EXPANDED ANIMATION SYSTEM

Create a large library of different animations to make gameplay feel natural and varied.

Avoid repeating the same animation every time an action occurs.

Running animations

- Normal running.
- Sprinting.
- Jogging.
- Side-stepping.
- Sudden direction changes.
- Acceleration.
- Deceleration.
- Turning while carrying the ball.
- Fatigued running.

Attacking animations

- Different passing animations.
- One-handed passes.
- Spin passes.
- Offloads during tackles.
- High-ball catching.
- Diving for the try line.
- Breaking through tackles.
- Hand-offs.
- Fending.
- Grubber kicks.
- Drop kicks.
- Place kicks.
- Cross-field kicks.

Defensive animations

- Standing tackles.
- Low tackles.
- Diving tackles.
- Big shoulder tackles.
- Missed tackles.
- Falling backwards.
- Getting dragged forward.
- Breaking free from tackles.
- Interceptions.
- Recovering from the ground.

Contact and breakdown animations

- Players falling naturally after collisions.
- Players getting back onto their feet.
- Ruck formation.
- Players driving into rucks.
- Maul formation.
- Players pushing and contesting possession.
- Ball presentation after a tackle.

Celebration animations

- Individual try celebrations.
- Teammates celebrating together.
- Group celebrations.
- Captain celebrations.
- Final whistle celebrations.
- World Cup trophy celebrations.

Animations should blend smoothly into one another and react to player movement, momentum and physical interactions.

6. PHYSICS AND ANIMATION INTERACTION

Animations must work together with the physics engine.

For example:

- A player running at full speed should have different tackle outcomes compared with a stationary player.
- A powerful player should be harder to stop in certain situations.
- A smaller, agile player should be able to sidestep larger defenders.
- A player being tackled should react according to the angle and strength of the collision.
- Players should not simply snap into predetermined positions.
- Ball movement should remain physics-driven.
- Players should maintain proper contact with the ground.
- Different body types should influence movement and collision behaviour.

Use animation blending, inverse kinematics and procedural movement where possible.

7. PORTRAIT MOBILE CONTROL INTERFACE

Design the entire gameplay interface specifically for vertical mobile screens.

Attacking layout

- Virtual joystick in the bottom-left.
- Pass button in the bottom-right.
- Sprint button.
- Kick button.
- Offload button.
- Fend/side-step button.
- Optional special action button.

Defensive layout

- Virtual joystick.
- Switch player button.
- Normal tackle button.
- Dive tackle button.
- Big tackle button.
- Interception/pressure button.

The interface should change automatically depending on possession.

Keep the scoreboard, match clock and score at the top of the screen.

Controls must not cover important gameplay areas or make players difficult to see.

Allow custom button layouts and adjustable control sensitivity.

8. FINAL DEVELOPMENT PRIORITIES

The most important requirements are:

1. Real historical rugby players, teams and statistics from 1975 to the present.
2. A genuine 3D side-view experience played vertically in portrait mode.
3. Direct manual control of the active player.
4. Automatic possession-based switching when passing.
5. Manual defender switching and selectable tackling techniques.
6. Extensive animations with natural transitions.
7. Physics-driven gameplay and realistic player interactions.
8. Optimised graphics for mobile devices.

IMPORTANT:
Integrate everything into the existing game.

Do not remove existing features, simplify existing systems or create non-functional placeholder buttons.

Do not use a top-down camera, landscape gameplay or flat 2D character models.

The final result should be a proper, playable, vertically designed 3D rugby simulation with deep historical content and responsive manual controls."

219: export function makeSquad(team, seedExtra = 0, options = {}) {
220:   const rng = rngFrom(hashString(team.id + ':' + seedExtra));
221:   const firsts = FIRSTS[team.pool] || FIRSTS.en;
222:   const lasts = SURNAMES[team.pool] || SURNAMES.en;
223:   const used = new Set();
224:   return POSITIONS.map((pos, idx) => {
225:     let first, last, name;
226:     do {
227:       first = firsts[Math.floor(rng() * firsts.length)];
228:       last = lasts[Math.floor(rng() * lasts.length)];
229:       name = `${first} ${last}`;
230:     } while (used.has(name));
231:     used.add(name);
232:     const prof = POSITION_PROFILE[pos.key] || POSITION_PROFILE.CTR;
233:     const base = team.rating - 4 + rng() * 8;
234:     const attrs = {};
235:     for (const a of ATTRS) {
236:       let v = base + (prof[a] || 0) + (rng() - .5) * 10;
237:       if (pos.group === 'BEN') v -= 3;
238:       attrs[a] = clamp(v);
239:     }
240:     attrs.stamina = clamp(attrs.stamina + 4, 40, 99);
241:     const player = {
242:       id: `${team.id}-${idx + 1}`,
243:       teamId: team.id,
244:       number: pos.n,
245:       position: pos.key,
246:       posName: pos.name,
247:       group: pos.group === 'BEN' ? 'BEN' : pos.group,
248:       name,
249:       age: 21 + Math.floor(rng() * 13),
250:       height: 176 + Math.floor(rng() * 30),
251:       weight: pos.group === 'FWD' ? 102 + Math.floor(rng() * 23) : 80 + Math.floor(rng() * 20),
252:       potential: clamp(72 + rng() * 22, 70, 99),
253:       ...attrs,
254:       form: 70 + Math.floor(rng() * 22),
255:       fitness: 88 + Math.floor(rng() * 12),
256:       morale: 75 + Math.floor(rng() * 20),
257:       xp: 0,
258:       injury: 0,
259:       suspension: 0,
260:       starter: pos.n <= 15,
261:       bench: pos.n > 15
262:     };
263:     player.overall = overallFor(player);
264:     return player;
265:   });
266: }

## Objective
- Build and verify a complete, mobile-first Rugby World Cup game with playable rugby simulation, tournament and career systems, touch controls, and saved progress.

## Requirements
- Prioritize mobile gameplay, rugby rules, physics, tactical AI, and stable performance.
- Include 15-a-side play, set pieces, tackles, passing, kicking, scoring, cards, substitutions, advantage, and referee decisions.
- Include World Cup, historical/custom tournaments, quick match, career, training, practice, and exhibition modes.
- Use lightweight deterministic Canvas gameplay and save tournament/career progress locally.

## Decisions
- Continue with the existing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript implementation.
- Retain the deterministic, physics-flavoured Canvas match engine.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented the app shell, match engine, renderer, tournament and career systems, data, audio, navigation, and responsive UI.
- Verified all `js/*.js` modules with `node --check`.
- Simulated tournament progression to completion and previously browser-tested a full World Cup with 48/48 matches played.
- Tested career season simulation, training points, lineup swap, development, and season completion; browser-tested career squad, tactics, training, and reload restoration.
- Added `favicon.svg` and linked it in `index.html`.
- Refreshed `screenshots/final-mobile.jpg`; career browser run reported no console or page errors.

### Active
- Further browser-test match gameplay paths: scoring/conversions, set pieces, cards, substitutions, and remaining rugby rules.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Exercise remaining match gameplay paths and check browser console/network errors.
2. Run any additional end-to-end sanity checks needed for the unverified rugby rules.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: App entry and favicon link.
- `favicon.svg`: Rugby-ball favicon.
- `js/app.js`: Navigation, mode orchestration, match controls, and UI actions.
- `js/engine.js`: Match physics, AI, rules, set pieces, and player actions.
- `js/renderer.js`: Canvas match presentation.
- `js/tournament.js`: Tournament generation and knockout progression.
- `js/career.js`: Career, player development, tactics, and season systems.
- `screenshots/final-mobile.jpg`: Refreshed mobile screenshot.
- `/tmp/opencode/career-check.cjs`: Playwright career UI and reload-persistence verification script.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; `git status --short` showed untracked `.gitignore`, `Agents.md`, scripts, `favicon.svg`, `index.html`, `js/`, and `styles.css`.
- App is served at `http://localhost:3002/`; browser testing used Chromium via CDP at `http://127.0.0.1:9222`.
- Save key: `rwc26_mobile_save_v2`.
- Career browser test selected England, tested squad development/autopick, tactics, and a training drill; after reload the career restored with training points saved.

function rngFrom(seed) {
  let a = seed >>> 0;
  return () => {
    a |= 0; a = a + 0x6D2B79F5 | 0;
    let t = Math.imul(a ^ a >>> 15, 1 | a);
    t = t + Math.imul(t ^ t >>> 7, 61 | t) ^ t;
    return ((t ^ t >>> 14) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
  };
}
export { rngFrom };

export function hashString(s) {
  let h = 2166136261;
  for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) { h ^= s.charCodeAt(i); h = Math.imul(h, 16777619); }
  return h >>> 0;
}

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Upgrade the existing Rugby World Cup game into a vertical, side-view 3D rugby simulation with deep historical content, direct manual controls, and expanded rugby systems while preserving all existing functionality.

## Requirements
- Add comprehensive real international rugby data from 1975 onward, including historical/current teams and players, eras, positions, ratings, caps, points, tries, kicking stats, tournament appearances, captains, and legendary players.
- Keep statistics accurate and clearly separate verified data from estimated gameplay ratings.
- Give every team distinctive AI tactics and formation behavior.
- Make portrait 9:16 gameplay mandatory, using an elevated side-on 3D camera with pitch depth, camera follow, zoom, and cinematic action framing.
- Replace top-down presentation with low-poly 3D players, stadiums, kits, crowds, advertising, balls, goalposts, lighting, shadows, and pitch detail.
- Add direct joystick control of the ball carrier, automatic control transfer after passes, responsive defending, defender switching, tackling types, and possession-specific controls.
- Add varied attacking, defensive, breakdown, running, and celebration animations with physics-driven reactions.
- Preserve the existing World Cup, career, quick match, training, tournament, exhibition, practice, save, and audio systems.

## Decisions
- Continue evolving the existing HTML/CSS/JavaScript implementation rather than replacing it.
- Preserve the deterministic, physics-flavoured match engine and existing tournament/career systems.
- Split new work into dedicated modules and use the existing canvas match loop for integration.
- Vendored Three.js is available for the 3D side-view presentation layer.

## Work State
### Completed
- Existing app shell, match engine, renderer, tournament and career systems, data, audio, navigation, saves, and responsive UI remain implemented.
- Existing controls include a virtual joystick, pass, sprint, kick, switch, and tackle actions.
- All `js/*.js` modules have previously passed `node --check`.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Upgrade the Rugby World Cup game into a portrait, side-view 3D rugby simulation with historical international data, direct controls, distinctive team AI, and expanded match systems.

## Requirements
- Add accurate 1975-present international history while clearly labeling estimated gameplay ratings.
- Preserve tournament, career, quick match, training, saves, audio, and existing match functionality.
- Make 9:16 portrait 3D gameplay mandatory with camera follow, zoom, stadium detail, and mobile controls.
- Preserve control transfer, pass/kick/tackle systems, set pieces, cards, substitutions, animations, and rugby rules.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing HTML/CSS/JavaScript implementation rather than replacing it.
- Keep the deterministic simulation engine and Canvas fallback.
- Integrate the Three.js presentation additively.
- Add dedicated historical/team-identity modules and retain the save key `rwc26_mobile_save_v2`.

## Work State
### Completed
- Existing app shell, engine, Canvas renderer, tournament, career, saves, audio, data, and navigation remain implemented.
- Three.js was downloaded to `vendor/three.module.js`.
- A large historical database module was created at `js/history.js`.
- The archive covers prominent eras and teams including New Zealand, South Africa, France, England, Ireland, Australia, Argentina, Scotland, Wales, Fiji, Italy, Japan, Samoa, Tonga, Georgia, Canada, USA, Uruguay, Namibia, Romania, Portugal, Spain, Chile, and Hong Kong.
- Team identities, formation behavior, tactical AI profiles, historic-era kits, public career records, player roles, honours, World Cup appearances, and estimated era ratings were added.
- The historical module distinguishes public career totals from gameplay estimates.

### Active
- Integrating `js/history.js` into the existing data/browser interfaces.
- Replacing or augmenting `MatchRenderer` with a genuine portrait 3D Three.js side-view scene.
- Completing control transfer and defender-switching behavior.
- Expanding tackle, pass, kick, breakdown, set-piece, and celebration presentation.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Import and expose historical players, eras, ratings, identities, and kits in `js/app.js` and `js/data.js`.
2. Replace or augment `js/renderer.js` with the Three.js side-view scene while retaining Canvas fallback.
3. Integrate possession-based automatic control transfer and manual defender switching.
4. Add 3D players, kits, pitch, stadium, crowd, boards, shadows, lighting, goalposts, ball, and reactions.
5. Browser-test portrait gameplay, 3D rendering, controls, scoring, set pieces, cards, substitutions, network errors, and console errors.
6. Refresh the mobile screenshot after 3D integration.

## Relevant Files
- `js/history.js`: Historical archive, team identities, kits, and player records.
- `js/renderer.js`: Existing Canvas presenter requiring Three.js integration or replacement.
- `js/app.js`: Match UI, navigation, browser interfaces, controls, and match orchestration.
- `js/engine.js`: Possession, tackling, set pieces, cards, substitutions, and match loop.
- `js/data.js`: Existing team, player, position, stadium, and legend datasets.
- `js/tournament.js`: World Cup and classic-tournament progression.
- `js/career.js`: Career progression and persistence.
- `styles.css`: Portrait 9:16 layout and match control styling.
- `index.html`: Application entry and module integration.
- `vendor/three.module.js`: Vendored Three.js rendering library.

## Important Context
- `js/history.js` is newly created and should be integrated rather than recreated.
- Three.js is vendored locally at `vendor/three.module.js`; no external network dependency should be required.
- The existing save format and key must remain unchanged.
- Changes remain uncommitted unless newer repository state differs.

## Process lifecycle

- Do not background them in bounded commands without explicit detachment and cleanup.
- After a timeout, inspect the process and endpoint before retrying or claiming failure.

## Linux browser and WebGPU capture

- Use the preinstalled `playwright-cli` executable from Actions or SSH.
- Use its headed Chromium, persistent Xvfb display, and SwiftShader configuration.
- Run `playwright-cli open http://localhost:3002` for the Pascal development server.
- Load a saved scene. Wait for actual geometry and the active WebGPU renderer.
- Run `playwright-cli screenshot --filename=screenshots/linux.png` after creating the output directory.
- Inspect the image. Reject loading screens, empty grids, and blank canvases.
- Report SwiftShader as CPU software rendering. Do not claim GPU hardware acceleration.
- Inspect `$HOME/.local/share/omgithub-playwright/linux.json` for launch settings.

messages.text:
"UPGRADE THE EXISTING RUGBY WORLD CUP GAME WITH THE FOLLOWING SYSTEMS. Do not create a separate game or replace existing working systems. Expand the existing game while preserving all current functionality.

1. HISTORICAL RUGBY DATABASE (1975–PRESENT)

Create a comprehensive historical rugby database covering international rugby from 1975 through to the present day.

Include real historical and modern:

- National teams.
- International players.
- Player names and positions.
- Player statistics and attributes.
- Team statistics and rankings.
- World Cup appearances.
- International caps.
- Tries scored.
- Points scored.
- Kicking statistics.
- Tournament performances.
- Captains and legendary players.

Include legendary players from different generations, alongside current international players.

Examples of players to include:

- Jonah Lomu
- Dan Carter
- Richie McCaw
- Bryan Habana
- Victor Matfield
- Joost van der Westhuizen
- François Pienaar
- Fourie du Preez
- Cheslin Kolbe
- Siya Kolisi
- Antoine Dupont
- Jonny Wilkinson
- Martin Johnson
- Brian O'Driscoll
- Sergio Parisse
- George Gregan
- David Campese
- Gareth Edwards
- JPR Williams

These are examples, not the complete database.

Historical accuracy

- Use real player names and historically accurate statistics wherever verified data is available.
- Player ratings must reflect actual playing abilities during their respective eras.
- Players must have different ratings depending on their career stage.
- A legendary player's prime version should have different attributes from their younger or older versions.
- Historical teams must use appropriate players, kits, team colours and playing styles from their respective periods.
- Include real historical national team squads and tournament rosters wherever data is available.
- Do not invent historical caps, tries, points or achievements.
- Clearly distinguish verified statistics from estimated gameplay ratings.

Allow players to browse historical teams and players by year, country, position and tournament.

2. NATIONAL TEAM IDENTITIES AND PLAYING STYLES

Every national team should have its own identity and tactical approach.

Examples:

SOUTH AFRICA:

- Physical forward play.
- Powerful scrums.
- Strong defensive structures.
- Tactical kicking.
- Dominant breakdown play.

NEW ZEALAND:

- Fast attacking rugby.
- Excellent handling.
- Dynamic running lines.
- Creative offloads.
- High-tempo gameplay.

FRANCE:

- Creative attacking rugby.
- Unpredictable attacking combinations.
- Strong individual flair.

ENGLAND:

- Structured gameplay.
- Strong forward pack.
- Tactical kicking.
- Organised defensive systems.

IRELAND:

- Structured attacking patterns.
- Accurate passing.
- Strong tactical organisation.

These playing styles should influence team AI, tactical tendencies, formations and player behaviour.

3. VERTICAL PORTRAIT GAMEPLAY AND 3D SIDE-VIEW CAMERA

THIS IS A MANDATORY REQUIREMENT.

The game must be played exclusively in VERTICAL PORTRAIT MODE (9:16).

Do not use landscape orientation.

Camera perspective

Create a genuine 3D side-view rugby experience designed around a vertically held mobile phone.

- Use a slightly elevated 3D side-view camera.
- Show players from a side-on perspective rather than looking down from above.
- The pitch should have visible depth and perspective.
- The camera should smoothly follow the active player and ball.
- Allow the camera to scroll along the pitch as the game progresses.
- Keep attacking and defensive players visible wherever possible.
- Use subtle camera zooms during important moments.
- Include cinematic camera adjustments during tries, tackles and major plays.

The game should feel like a 3D rugby simulation viewed from the side, not a 2D rugby game or a top-down strategy game.

Graphics style

Use polished, stylised LOW-POLY 3D graphics.

The graphics should be noticeably better than basic placeholder graphics without requiring photorealistic rendering.

Include:

- Fully modelled 3D rugby players.
- Different body types and physical proportions.
- Recognisable player faces and hairstyles where possible.
- Fully modelled 3D stadiums.
- 3D rugby balls.
- Detailed goalposts.
- Textured rugby pitches.
- Realistic player kits and numbers.
- Stadium crowds.
- Advertising boards.
- Benches and coaching areas.
- Dynamic lighting and shadows.
- Visible grass and pitch markings.

The characters must look like proper 3D human rugby players, not flat sprites or 2D cutouts.

Prioritise smooth performance on mid-range Android devices.

4. COMPLETE MANUAL PLAYER-CONTROL SYSTEM

THIS IS EXTREMELY IMPORTANT.

The user must directly control the players on their team.

Do not make the team play entirely through automatic AI.

Attacking controls

When the user's team has possession:

- The player carrying the ball becomes the actively controlled character.
- The user controls that player's movement using a virtual joystick.
- The user decides when to sprint, change direction, pass, kick or attempt to break through defenders.
- The user controls the direction and timing of passes.
- When the ball is passed, control must automatically transfer to the receiving player once possession is established.
- The receiving player immediately becomes the actively controlled character.
- The user can continue running, passing, kicking or performing other actions with the new ball carrier.

This must happen smoothly and immediately.

Supporting players

Other teammates should still move intelligently, but must not take control away from the user.

- AI teammates should run support lines.
- Players should create attacking space.
- Wingers should stay wide when appropriate.
- Forwards should provide support around breakdowns.
- Teammates should position themselves for offloads and passes.
- AI should recognise opportunities to support the ball carrier.

The user remains in control of the player with the ball.

Defensive controls

When the opposing team has possession:

- Allow the user to switch between all available defensive players.
- Add a dedicated player-switch button.
- Highlight the currently selected defender.
- Allow manual switching using repeated button presses or directional selection.
- The selected player becomes directly controlled by the user.

The user decides how to defend.

Include different defensive actions:

1. NORMAL TACKLE – a standard standing tackle.
2. DIVE TACKLE – a diving attempt to bring down an opponent.
3. LOW TACKLE – targeting the legs.
4. BIG TACKLE – a stronger tackle attempt requiring appropriate timing and positioning.
5. INTERCEPTION – attempting to intercept a pass.
6. DEFENSIVE PRESSURE – closing down the ball carrier.

Different tackling actions must have different animations, physics, success rates and risks.

A poorly timed tackle should have consequences, including missed tackles, broken tackles, players being sidestepped or penalties where appropriate.

Player switching intelligence

- Highlight the currently selected player.
- Make switching responsive.
- Allow quick switching to the nearest relevant defender.
- Never force the user to stay with one defender.
- Switching must not interrupt the flow of gameplay.

5. EXPANDED ANIMATION SYSTEM

Create a large library of different animations to make gameplay feel natural and varied.

Avoid repeating the same animation every time an action occurs.

Running animations

- Normal running.
- Sprinting.
- Jogging.
- Side-stepping.
- Sudden direction changes.
- Acceleration.
- Deceleration.
- Turning while carrying the ball.
- Fatigued running.

Attacking animations

- Different passing animations.
- One-handed passes.
- Spin passes.
- Offloads during tackles.
- High-ball catching.
- Diving for the try line.
- Breaking through tackles.
- Hand-offs.
- Fending.
- Grubber kicks.
- Drop kicks.
- Place kicks.
- Cross-field kicks.

Defensive animations

- Standing tackles.
- Low tackles.
- Diving tackles.
- Big shoulder tackles.
- Missed tackles.
- Falling backwards.
- Getting dragged forward.
- Breaking free from tackles.
- Interceptions.
- Recovering from the ground.

Contact and breakdown animations

- Players falling naturally after collisions.
- Players getting back onto their feet.
- Ruck formation.
- Players driving into rucks.
- Maul formation.
- Players pushing and contesting possession.
- Ball presentation after a tackle.

Celebration animations

- Individual try celebrations.
- Teammates celebrating together.
- Group celebrations.
- Captain celebrations.
- Final whistle celebrations.
- World Cup trophy celebrations.

Animations should blend smoothly into one another and react to player movement, momentum and physical interactions.

6. PHYSICS AND ANIMATION INTERACTION

Animations must work together with the physics engine.

For example:

- A player running at full speed should have different tackle outcomes compared with a stationary player.
- A powerful player should be harder to stop in certain situations.
- A smaller, agile player should be able to sidestep larger defenders.
- A player being tackled should react according to the angle and strength of the collision.
- Players should not simply snap into predetermined positions.
- Ball movement should remain physics-driven.
- Players should maintain proper contact with the ground.
- Different body types should influence movement and collision behaviour.

Use animation blending, inverse kinematics and procedural movement where possible.

7. PORTRAIT MOBILE CONTROL INTERFACE

Design the entire gameplay interface specifically for vertical mobile screens.

Attacking layout

- Virtual joystick in the bottom-left.
- Pass button in the bottom-right.
- Sprint button.
- Kick button.
- Offload button.
- Fend/side-step button.
- Optional special action button.

Defensive layout

- Virtual joystick.
- Switch player button.
- Normal tackle button.
- Dive tackle button.
- Big tackle button.
- Interception/pressure button.

The interface should change automatically depending on possession.

Keep the scoreboard, match clock and score at the top of the screen.

Controls must not cover important gameplay areas or make players difficult to see.

Allow custom button layouts and adjustable control sensitivity.

8. FINAL DEVELOPMENT PRIORITIES

The most important requirements are:

1. Real historical rugby players, teams and statistics from 1975 to the present.
2. A genuine 3D side-view experience played vertically in portrait mode.
3. Direct manual control of the active player.
4. Automatic possession-based switching when passing.
5. Manual defender switching and selectable tackling techniques.
6. Extensive animations with natural transitions.
7. Physics-driven gameplay and realistic player interactions.
8. Optimised graphics for mobile devices.

IMPORTANT:
Integrate everything into the existing game.

Do not remove existing features, simplify existing systems or create non-functional placeholder buttons.

Do not use a top-down camera, landscape gameplay or flat 2D character models.

The final result should be a proper, playable, vertically designed 3D rugby simulation with deep historical content and responsive manual controls."

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Upgrade the existing Rugby World Cup game into a portrait, side-view 3D rugby simulation with historical international data, direct controls, distinctive team AI, and expanded match systems.

## Requirements
- Cover international history from 1975 onward and clearly distinguish public records from estimated gameplay ratings.
- Preserve tournament, career, quick match, training, saves, audio, and existing match functionality.
- Make 9:16 portrait 3D gameplay mandatory, with camera follow, zoom, stadium detail, and mobile controls.
- Preserve control transfer, pass/kick/tackle systems, set pieces, cards, substitutions, animations, and rugby rules.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing HTML/CSS/JavaScript game; retain the deterministic simulation engine and Canvas fallback.
- Integrate vendored Three.js additively.
- Keep the existing save key `rwc26_mobile_save_v2`.

## Work State
### Completed
- Created `js/history.js` with a 575-player archive, era data, World Cup records/finals, Five/Six Nations history, estimated era team ratings, estimated player attributes, and historical squad generation.
- Added archive navigation and views in `js/app.js` for World Cups, eras, nations, legends, dream fixtures, and championship history, plus archive player/team/era actions.
- Created `js/renderer3d.js` and added a Three.js-first renderer wrapper with Canvas fallback in `js/renderer.js`.
- Added renderer disposal on match stop.
- Updated `js/engine.js` with possession-based control transfer, a manual defender-switch lock/cooldown, and a switch control in the match UI.
- Added historical squads to tournament match launches when an edition year is available.

### Active
- Validate historical archive data, team identities/kits, and historical squad selection against the app’s actual team IDs and tournament flow.
- Finish and verify 3D rendering, including portrait camera behavior, controls, set-piece/score reactions, and renderer fallback.
- Complete and browser-test control, gameplay, and archive interactions.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Run syntax checks and inspect the current changes; fix any integration errors in `js/app.js`, `js/engine.js`, and both renderers.
2. Verify historical team IDs/data, squad selection, archive modals/actions, and tournament edition handling.
3. Browser-test portrait 3D gameplay, camera follow/zoom, mobile controls, possession switching, scoring, set pieces, cards, substitutions, Canvas fallback, network errors, and console errors.
4. Refresh the mobile screenshot and report validation results.

## Relevant Files
- `js/history.js`: Historical records, archive players, era ratings, and historical squad generation.
- `js/renderer3d.js`: New Three.js side-view match renderer.
- `js/renderer.js`: 3D renderer wrapper and existing Canvas fallback.
- `js/app.js`: Archive UI, match orchestration, and input handling.
- `js/engine.js`: Simulation and manual/automatic player control.
- `js/tournament.js`: Tournament edition and fixture progression.
- `js/data.js`: Existing team and player datasets.
- `styles.css`: Portrait layout and match controls.
- `vendor/three.module.js`: Vendored Three.js module.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; the earlier repository status showed `js/history.js` and `vendor/` as untracked, and later work added/modified more files.
- `js/app.js` now imports archive exports from `js/history.js`; verify all imported symbols and UI action cases are present and consistent.
- Historical squad ratings were adjusted using era-specific team baselines after initial generated ratings were too high; archive gameplay ratings/attributes are intended as estimates, not verified historical facts.
- The save key must remain `rwc26_mobile_save_v2`.

"UPGRADE THE EXISTING RUGBY WORLD CUP GAME WITH THE FOLLOWING SYSTEMS. Do not create a separate game or replace existing working systems. Expand the existing game while preserving all current functionality.

1. HISTORICAL RUGBY DATABASE (1975–PRESENT)

Create a comprehensive historical rugby database covering international rugby from 1975 through to the present day.

Include real historical and modern:

- National teams.
- International players.
- Player names and positions.
- Player statistics and attributes.
- Team statistics and rankings.
- World Cup appearances.
- International caps.
- Tries scored.
- Points scored.
- Kicking statistics.
- Tournament performances.
- Captains and legendary players.

Include legendary players from different generations, alongside current international players.

Examples of players to include:

- Jonah Lomu
- Dan Carter
- Richie McCaw
- Bryan Habana
- Victor Matfield
- Joost van der Westhuizen
- François Pienaar
- Fourie du Preez
- Cheslin Kolbe
- Siya Kolisi
- Antoine Dupont
- Jonny Wilkinson
- Martin Johnson
- Brian O'Driscoll
- Sergio Parisse
- George Gregan
- David Campese
- Gareth Edwards
- JPR Williams

These are examples, not the complete database.

Historical accuracy

- Use real player names and historically accurate statistics wherever verified data is available.
- Player ratings must reflect actual playing abilities during their respective eras.
- Players must have different ratings depending on their career stage.
- A legendary player's prime version should have different attributes from their younger or older versions.
- Historical teams must use appropriate players, kits, team colours and playing styles from their respective periods.
- Include real historical national team squads and tournament rosters wherever data is available.
- Do not invent historical caps, tries, points or achievements.
- Clearly distinguish verified statistics from estimated gameplay ratings.

Allow players to browse historical teams and players by year, country, position and tournament.

2. NATIONAL TEAM IDENTITIES AND PLAYING STYLES

Every national team should have its own identity and tactical approach.

Examples:

SOUTH AFRICA:

- Physical forward play.
- Powerful scrums.
- Strong defensive structures.
- Tactical kicking.
- Dominant breakdown play.

NEW ZEALAND:

- Fast attacking rugby.
- Excellent handling.
- Dynamic running lines.
- Creative offloads.
- High-tempo gameplay.

FRANCE:

- Creative attacking rugby.
- Unpredictable attacking combinations.
- Strong individual flair.

ENGLAND:

- Structured gameplay.
- Strong forward pack.
- Tactical kicking.
- Organised defensive systems.

IRELAND:

- Structured attacking patterns.
- Accurate passing.
- Strong tactical organisation.

These playing styles should influence team AI, tactical tendencies, formations and player behaviour.

3. VERTICAL PORTRAIT GAMEPLAY AND 3D SIDE-VIEW CAMERA

THIS IS A MANDATORY REQUIREMENT.

The game must be played exclusively in VERTICAL PORTRAIT MODE (9:16).

Do not use landscape orientation.

Camera perspective

Create a genuine 3D side-view rugby experience designed around a vertically held mobile phone.

- Use a slightly elevated 3D side-view camera.
- Show players from a side-on perspective rather than looking down from above.
- The pitch should have visible depth and perspective.
- The camera should smoothly follow the active player and ball.
- Allow the camera to scroll along the pitch as the game progresses.
- Keep attacking and defensive players visible wherever possible.
- Use subtle camera zooms during important moments.
- Include cinematic camera adjustments during tries, tackles and major plays.

The game should feel like a 3D rugby simulation viewed from the side, not a 2D rugby game or a top-down strategy game.

Graphics style

Use polished, stylised LOW-POLY 3D graphics.

The graphics should be noticeably better than basic placeholder graphics without requiring photorealistic rendering.

Include:

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Upgrade the existing Rugby World Cup game into a portrait 3D rugby simulation with historical international data, direct controls, distinctive team AI, and expanded match systems.
- Preserve the existing game and its tournament, career, quick match, training, save, audio, and match functionality.

## Requirements
- Cover international rugby from 1975 onward; distinguish verified public records from estimated gameplay ratings.
- Require 9:16 portrait gameplay with a side-view 3D camera, follow/zoom, stadium detail, and mobile controls.
- Preserve possession-based control transfer, manual defending, passes/kicks/tackles, set pieces, cards, substitutions, animations, and rugby rules.
- Browse historical teams and players by year, country, position, and tournament.
- Do not replace existing systems or leave controls nonfunctional.

## Decisions
- Extend the existing HTML/CSS/JavaScript game; retain the simulation engine and Canvas fallback.
- Integrate vendored Three.js additively.
- Keep the save key `rwc26_mobile_save_v2`.
- Treat historical gameplay ratings and attributes as estimates, not verified historical facts.

## Work State
### Completed
- Added `js/history.js` with a 575-player archive, era data, World Cup records/finals, Five/Six Nations history, estimated team ratings, player attributes, and historical squad generation.
- Added archive views/actions in `js/app.js` for World Cups, eras, nations, legends, dream fixtures, championships, and archive-player/team/era actions.
- Added legend archive filters for year, position group, and nation.
- Added a Three.js-first renderer wrapper with Canvas fallback and disposal on match stop.
- Added historical kit palettes, player body proportions and facial details, varied action/celebration animation poses, benches/coaching areas, and instanced grass detail to `js/renderer3d.js`.
- Added manual tackle types (`normal`, `low`, `dive`, `big`, `intercept`, `pressure`), missed-tackle consequences, fend and sidestep actions, tackle/celebration animation state, and tactical identity/formation influence in `js/engine.js`.
- Added possession-sensitive attack/defence control pads and action handlers in `js/app.js`.
- Added possession-based controlled-player transfer, defender switching, and historical squads for tournament match launches when an edition year is available.
- Ran `node --check` on `js/engine.js`, `js/app.js`, and `js/renderer3d.js` successfully before the latest UI/rendering edits.

### Active
- Re-run syntax checks after the latest edits and inspect integration points, especially tackle controls, archive filters, renderer animation properties, and team identity tactical fields.
- Validate historical team IDs/data, squad selection, archive actions, and tournament edition handling.
- Browser-test portrait 3D gameplay, camera follow/zoom, mobile controls, possession switching, tackles, scoring, set pieces, cards, substitutions, Canvas fallback, network errors, and console errors.
- Refresh the mobile screenshot and report validation results.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Run syntax checks on changed JavaScript files and fix any integration errors introduced by the latest edits.
2. Verify manual tackle calls and action buttons against existing engine methods, and ensure the new archive filters render and persist correctly.
3. Validate historical IDs, squads, kits, team AI, renderer fallback, and tournament edition flow.
4. Browser-test portrait gameplay and all major controls/match systems; inspect console/network errors and refresh the mobile screenshot.

## Relevant Files
- `js/history.js`: Historical records, archive players, team identities/kits, and historical squad generation.
- `js/renderer3d.js`: Three.js match renderer, stadium detail, kits, and player animations.
- `js/renderer.js`: Three.js renderer wrapper and Canvas fallback.
- `js/app.js`: Archive UI, match orchestration, mobile control pads, and input handling.
- `js/engine.js`: Match simulation, player control, tackles, and team tactics.
- `js/tournament.js`: Tournament edition and fixture progression.
- `js/data.js`: Existing team/player datasets and historical editions.
- `styles.css`: Portrait layout and match controls.
- `vendor/three.module.js`: Vendored Three.js module.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; earlier status showed `js/history.js` and `vendor/` untracked, with subsequent edits to additional files.
- Latest edits were not covered by the earlier successful syntax check.
- Confirm `IDENTITY_BY_TEAM[team.id].ai` values and `HISTORIC_KITS[team.id]` keys match actual team IDs before relying on them.
- Preserve the save key `rwc26_mobile_save_v2`.
